description: Galvanised steel lighting column with two opposed curved arms and a cobra-head lantern on each, for a central median

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Tall galvanised steel lighting column, octagonal in section and tapering as it rises from a wide square bolted base flange, a flat rectangular access door plate low on the shaft, and at the top a symmetrical pair of smooth curved outreach arms sweeping out to opposite sides and levelling off at equal height, each arm carrying on its end a closed cobra-head lantern housing shaped as a broad wedge that is deep at the arm and tapers to a shallow rounded nose with a single flat clear lens panel underneath Materials: Hot-dip galvanised steel gone dull matt grey with white zinc bloom, running rust streaks below the access door and around the base bolts, road grime and splash darkening the lowest metre, grey painted lantern housings chalky on the sunward side, insect debris behind the lenses.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless pure WHITE studio matte. The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless white backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient. This is a studio cut-out, NOT an outdoor photograph: there must be no sky, no clouds, no buildings, no road and no overhead cables anywhere in the frame.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo. The lamp is switched OFF and emits no light.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: Final measured cost against all four ceilings. Measured bbox 5.2 x 9.97 x 0.4 m. Cost: 1240 triangles / 16000, 5 draw calls / 12, 3 materials / 8, 5 unique geometries / 16, 1 textures. Turntable gate passes on all four azimuths (segmented, holed false, silhouette ratios [1.0, 0.717, 0.999, 0.716], interior hole fractions [0.0022, 0.0025, 0.0036, 0.0037]).  Five components at 5 draw calls, 3 materials and 5 geometries against a hero2x ceiling of 12/8/16 -- deliberately underspent, as this asset's own notes argue for a prop placed in runs down a median.

featureReviews.notes: Measured bbox 5.20 x 9.97 x 0.40 m against the declared 5.2 x 10 x 0.4 -- exact on width and depth, 0.3% under on height. Width is set by the two lantern noses at +-2.60 m and depth by the baseplate, both landed deliberately. Proportion comes from the DECLARATION, not the plate: the plate's shaft is 0.177 of its own span, which at 5.2 m would be a 0.92 m shaft against the 0.22 m the asset notes state.

Both arms rise from ONE banded collar at the shaft top and curve out symmetrically as eased quarter-turns -- tight at the top, straight along the outreach, which is the shape of a real bracket arm and what the plate shows. The previous build was two thin wires off a smooth pipe with no collar to rise from. Arm radius 0.055, below the single-arm cobra's 0.062, because a median column carries two lighter arms.

A 0.70 m cast wedge on each arm, deepest at the spigot (0.150 m) and tapering to the nose (0.086 m), each over an acrylic refractor bowl hung proud of the casting, and each with the stepped spigot collar the plate shows where the arm enters. A plain box reads as a shoebox on a stick; the taper is the cobra.

An EIGHT-segment lathe, not twelve: the plate's column reads octagonal and the previous build shipped a round pipe. It tapers r 0.110 to 0.075 and flares to r 0.168 over the bottom 0.60 m where it meets its plate -- the plate's column is visibly much wider at the foot than under the collar, and that flare is most of what reads as a structural column.

Three material layers: galvanised #949c9e measured off the plate's subject mask (p25 119,122,127 / p50 134,139,143 / p75 169,173,174), cast aluminium #a6abab for the luminaires -- lighter and smoother, which is the only thing separating them from the column at street level -- and acrylic #d6dad4 at roughness 0.20. Luma 138 is well clear of the 55.5-60.5 band gatecrop's alpha key erases, so no lift was needed. NOT carried: the plate's heavy directional staining down one face and the long rust run below the hand-hole; the tile is isotropic, which is why this is 0.90.

A 0.40 m square plate -- the declared depth exactly -- with four PROUD 55 mm hex bolts, which is what the plate shows rather than the flush studs the cobra head uses. The previous build had no baseplate at all. The bolted hand-hole door at 1.05 m sits on the shaft component.

name: Steel Twin-Arm Street Lamp

notes:
The central-median version, one lantern over each carriageway. Sized from a 10 m mounting height with 2.5 m of outreach each side, which is what the 5.2 m width is: the shaft is about 0.22 m across at the base. budgetClass pinned to hero against the hero2x its 10 m height would derive, because the prop is two tapered cylinders and a mirrored arm-and-lantern assembly that instances -- the second arm should cost a transform, not a second set of geometry -- and these are placed in long runs down a dual carriageway where 16k triangles and 12 draw calls each would dominate the frame. The plate scaffold pushes against thin forms, so the prompt describes the arms as continuous chunky sweeps and asks for no cabling or fixings hanging off them. Static: bolted to a foundation, so physics stays disabled.

BUDGET CLASS RAISED hero -> hero2x (2026-08-31), one step, as part of the lighting-kit rebuild to a fidelity above 0.92. The lighting props were authored to ceilings that could not carry their identity features -- the bulkhead's guard cage is the clearest case: as one lathe inside 800 triangles the only guard expressible is two circumferential bands, and it rendered as a stack of pale discs. The extra room is a CEILING, not a target: every one of these is still built by merging parts into as few components as possible, so draw calls, materials and unique geometries stay far below the new class and only triangles are actually spent.
